new_statements.quote: [p.33] Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic-a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit that is constructed from a restricted set of segments. The minorsyllable typically consists of an oral stop or fricative of unmarked phonation type, an epenthetic ([a] or schwa-like) vowel, and may be closed by a nasal or rhotic. [p.26] The Oi are often known by their village name, and various terms in the literature which actually refer to the same languages, such as The, Thang Ong and Sok [...] [p.28] The minorsyllables are robust, with Oi frequently preserving Cər and Cən types.
new_statements.citation: Sidwell, Paul & Pascale Jacq. 2003. A Handbook of Comparative Bahnaric, Vol. 1: West Bahnaric. (Pacific Linguistics 551.) Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, The Australian National University.

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the copies we hold under (symlinks). (1) Sidwell & Jacq 2003, PL-551: the p.33 sentence is at lines 1838-1842 and on p.43 (printed p.33, sec. 4.2 'PWB phonological word'): 'Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic-a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit that is constructed from a restricted set of segments. The minorsyllable typically consists of an oral stop or fricative of unmarked phonation type, an epenthetic ([a] or schwa-like) vowel, and may be closed by a nasal or rhotic.' -- verbatim (only scanned spacing artefacts, e.g. 'c losed'). The p.26 identity sentence…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (minor syllable + main syllable); in sesquisyllables the final, main syllable carries the stress and the preceding minor syllable is unstressed/reduced (iambic pattern). Stated for West Bahnaric languages as a group; the Oi profile (which explicitly subsumes 'The') describes robust minor syllables with an [a]-coloured epenthetic vowel but gives no separate stress sentence.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Oi/The. (The WB-wide statement is hedged 'Most WB languages'; the known exception discussed elsewhere is Nyaheun's monosyllabicization, not Oi.) Daniell 2020 p.4 adds for Inthii Oy that minor syllables are shorter and lower-pitched than the main syllable (209 vs 235 Hz), consistent with main-syllable prominence.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (mono-/sesquisyllabic lexical words, citation forms in a comparative handbook); no phrase-level prosody discussed. Statement is branch-level (West Bahnaric), applied to Oi (= Oy, incl. Ban The) by inclusion, not an Oi-specific instrumental finding.
new_statements.identity_note: 'The' (thee1240, retired ISO [thx]) is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry retired in 2015 as a duplicate of Oy [oyb] = Glottolog oyyy1238 (ISO CR 2014-014: 'Oy and The are the same language', two villages across the river from each other, 97% lexical similarity). Sidwell & Jacq 2003 treat The as a village name of the Oi (p.6 fn.2: 'There is an Oi community who call their village Ban The, and it is called Ban Tha in Lao.. residents.. call themselves Oi-The and even The-Oi'; p.26). The quoted stress statement is the West-Bahnaric-wide sentence of PL-551 sec. 4.2, applied to Oi/The by inclusion; Daniell 2020 describes the Inthii village variety of Oy, not Ban The. Any catalog entry should be filed under oyyy1238 (Oy) rather than as a separate language.

sources.note: p.6 fn.2 and sec. 3.7 pp.26-28 identify 'The' as an Oi village/name ('various terms in the literature which actually refer to the same languages, such as The, Thang Ong and Sok'; Jacq's 1998 fieldwork ran 'from Ban Lagnao to Ban The'). Oi profile gives inventories and 'The minorsyllables are robust.. minorsyllable vowel, whether phonemic or epenthetic, tends to be clearly vocalised as [a]' but no Oi-specific stress sentence. Sec. 4.2 p.33: 'Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic.. a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable' = word-final (main-syllable) stress stated for West Bahnari…

sources.citation: Daniell, Jennifer L. 2020. A look at diachronic phonological processes in Inthii Oy. JSEALS 13.1: 1-11 + word-list appendix (hdl 10524/52459).
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Inthii village variety of Oy (not Ban The). The word 'stress' is not used; p.4 sec.3.1: minor syllables are identified by 'duration and intonatory patterns, i.e. the main syllable being of a relatively higher pitch than the minor syllable' (F0 209 vs 235 Hz; 210 vs 229 Hz). p.2 lists 'The' among West Bahnaric lects (after Sidwell 2009) and cites Sidwell & Jacq 2003:33 on robust sesquisyllabicity. Refers to Daniell 2019 MA thesis for the full synchronic phonology of four Oy varieties.

sources.note: 'The' and 'Oy' appear only in the genetic index ('OI-THE: Jeng, Oy, Sok, Sapuan, The'); no language-specific statement. Mon-Khmer generalization: 'The most obvious recurring accent pattern in the Mon-Khmer languages relates to the canonical sesquisyllabic word structure which implies the iambic rhythm of an unaccented presyllable and an accented main syllable.'
